_about: Tiny curated guidance corpus for single-pass RAG grounding of the LUCID-PD explanation layer (RQ3). Snippets paraphrase public NICE NG71 and NHS guidance plus general clinical statements. Sources are indicative; verify exact wording against the cited document before any non-research use.

snippets.text: Parkinson's disease is diagnosed clinically, from a person's symptoms, examination and history. There is no single laboratory or imaging test that confirms it on its own.
If Parkinson's disease is suspected, refer the person, untreated, to a specialist with expertise in the differential diagnosis of the condition rather than starting treatment first.
People with suspected Parkinson's disease should be seen by a specialist quickly, within a few weeks of referral, so that diagnosis and management can begin without undue delay.
Common early features of Parkinson's include tremor, slowness of movement and muscle stiffness. Changes in speech, handwriting and facial expression can also occur.
Parkinsonian speech can show reduced loudness, a monotone or breathy voice quality, imprecise articulation and altered timing. These voice changes are the signal that voice-based screening measures.
Parkinson's disease is a long-term progressive neurological condition. Care is multidisciplinary and tailored to the individual over time.
A screening or decision-support tool can highlight people who may benefit from specialist assessment. It does not make a diagnosis and does not replace a clinician's judgement.

A risk estimate indicates the strength of evidence for further assessment, not a confirmed diagnosis. A higher estimate means specialist review is more strongly indicated; it is not proof that the disease is present.
